quotes.quote: Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next.

We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties.

MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol.
MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures.

For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings.
Molecular structures. Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.
Scientific reasoning. Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another.
Ranking and selection. Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements.
Property predictions. Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties.
Predictions receive partial credit based on their closeness to the measured values. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly.
We evaluated eleven GPT models at different reasoning-effort settings.
Each point represents a model at one reasoning setting, showing 51 combinations across nine models from GPT‑5.6 onward. Scores are averaged across 99 problems; bars show 95% uncertainty intervals.
While measuring the benchmark for structure components, Astra earned 95.4% of the available credit at xhigh.

Where selection and prediction remain difficult, Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh, but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties.

These results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments.

MedChemBench: Evaluating complex multimodal reasoning in medicinal chemistry
Jeremy Li1,† , Andrew Ho1 , Suyash Shringarpure1,† , Amelia Liu1 , Paul Humphries1 , Joy Jiao1 … 1 OpenAI … November 9, 2026
Here we introduce MedChemBench (MCB), a retrospective multimodal benchmark comprising 99 medicinal chemistry problems based on cases reported in recent papers and patents
MCB evaluates how models combine molecular and experimental evidence to reason through decisions encountered in medicinal chemistry programs.

Here we introduce MedChemBench (MCB), a new 99-problem benchmark for AI models with a retrospective setup based on 117 recently published scientific papers and patent publications, spanning 761 distinct graded molecular structures.
The highest mean score was 83.83%, achieved by GPT-6 Astra at max effort. At xhigh effort, a setting evaluated for all eleven models, scores ranged from 35.02% to 83.33%.
GPT-6 Astra at max achieved the highest observed mean score, 83.83% (interval, 81.27–86.20%).
GPT-5.6 Sol earned 58.23%, exceeding GPT-5.5 by 8.97 percentage points.
At xhigh, molecular structure scores showed the widest range across models: GPT-6 Astra earned 95.37% of available structure credit, GPT-6.1 Sol and Terra earned 93.70% and 92.18%, respectively
The tasks cover preclinical drug discovery; clinical development is outside the benchmark’s scope.
Domain annotations are author-derived and nonexclusive: a task can span potency, ADME, structure-guided reasoning, and other domains. Eighty-five of the 99 tasks span more than one domain.

We use RDKit to convert submitted SMILES strings to canonical isomeric SMILES, preserving specified stereochemistry and isotopes … An exact match receives full credit; mismatched, invalid, or missing structures receive zero credit.
The ranking score is the mean credit across the remaining pairs; missing, repeated, or unknown compounds receive zero credit. In this approach, a uniformly random ordering has expected credit of 0.5.
When a criterion asks for a specific set of candidates, credit is the Jaccard similarity between the predicted set P and reference set R: |P ∩ R|/|P ∪ R|.
Most numerical predictions receive partial credit based on fold error: an exact prediction earns full credit, while a prediction that is twice or half the reference value earns half credit.
For 202 criteria with positive predictions p and reference values t, credit is min(p, t)/ max(p, t).

A separate GPT-6 Astra judge at medium reasoning effort scores the scientific rationale criteria. The judge receives the question text and images, the criterion and grading guidance, and the submitted answer.
Each criterion earns zero, half, or full credit according to its task-specific scoring anchors.

For each model–effort condition, we divide a response’s earned points by the task’s full budget, average the ten retained responses with completed invalid outputs scored at zero, and then average all 99 tasks equally. Larger rubrics therefore do not give tasks more weight across the benchmark.
Each task is normalized to a maximum score of 1. Component shares are the mean fractions of that available score across all 99 tasks, including zero where a component is absent.
Component points are normalized within each applicable task, averaged across its responses, and then averaged equally across applicable tasks (92, 91, 86, and 21 tasks in C–F, respectively).
Pointwise 95% percentile intervals use 5,000 nonparametric task-bootstrap samples, with independent resamples for each model–effort condition and metric.
Although the sources for the 99 problems are relatively recent (median publication year, 2025), we were concerned that memorization could contribute to the stronger performance of more recent models.

Mean overall score changes after adding the source DOI or patent identifier ranged from −0.23 to +0.80 percentage points. All model-specific 95% confidence intervals included zero (10,000 paired bootstrap resamples of source groups), and model rankings remained unchanged.
explicitly identifying the source produced little average performance benefit, but this test cannot establish whether source material was present in training data.

The benchmark is also close to saturation in its current form: GPT-6 Astra achieved 83.83% at max reasoning effort. Future versions will need to be more challenging to continue distinguishing model performance.
Further validation should assess whether benchmark grading agrees with independent medicinal chemists’ evaluations of alternative approaches
the single-turn protocol measures performance with a fixed evidence package and does not assess recovery through computation, additional evidence, or iterative revision.
A complementary agent-based track should allow models to retrieve information, calculate molecular properties, verify structures, and revise proposals over multiple steps
Completed invalid responses and refusals were retained at zero credit; missing responses or grades were not scored as zero.
GPT-6 Sol and Luna were evaluated before the provider’s September 2026 image-encoding fix; its effect on these results was not measured (OpenAI API changelog).
Each model response was generated in a single turn. Models received text and images in the specified order and were instructed to return strict JSON with one top-level answer object.
selected sources that described a clear medicinal chemistry question and provided enough evidence to reconstruct a compound series or design problem.
Results reported later in the source publication are withheld from the prompt and used to inform reference answers and grading criteria.

GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6.1 Terra. Each of the 61 model–effort conditions contains ten retained responses for each of 99 tasks, giving 60,390 responses.
Each task combines prose with images of molecular structures, assay tables, plots, design diagrams, or protein-ligand complexes.

The 99 MCB tasks are grouped into seven primary categories (Table 1): (1) integrated lead selection, (2) SAR forecasting, (3) ADME and delivery, (4) safety and liabilities, (5) molecular design and enumeration, (6) assay biology and mechanism, and (7) retrosynthesis.
